# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review of Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Management

## Introduction and Epidemiology
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a rare but life-threatening form of heart failure that affects women of childbearing age [1]. It is defined as an idiopathic cardiomyopathy presenting with heart failure secondary to left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction, typically with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) < 45%, occurring toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, in the absence of other identifiable causes of heart failure [1,2]. The global incidence of PPCM varies widely, with the highest rates reported in Nigeria and Haiti, while it remains less common but is increasingly recognized in Western nations [2,3]. Well-established risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestations, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (such as preeclampsia), and African ancestry [4,5].

## Pathophysiology
Historically thought to be an inflammatory or autoimmune myocarditis, PPCM is now understood to be a vascular-hormonal disease triggered by late-pregnancy physiology in genetically susceptible individuals [6]. A central mechanism involves oxidative stress and the proteolytic cleavage of prolactin. In the third trimester, elevated oxidative stress leads to the activation of cathepsin D, which cleaves the nursing hormone prolactin (23 kDa) into a vasculotoxic and pro-apoptotic 16-kDa fragment [7,8]. This 16-kDa prolactin fragment impairs endothelial cell function, induces capillary regression, and triggers myocardial microvascular damage [8]. This pathway operates in tandem with an angiogenic imbalance. Near delivery, the placenta secretes high levels of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1), an anti-angiogenic protein that neutralizes vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), exacerbating systemic and myocardial endothelial dysfunction [9].

Genetics also play a foundational role in PPCM. Up to 15% to 20% of affected women harbor pathogenic variants in genes associated with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) [10]. Truncating variants in the titin gene (*TTN*) are the most common genetic finding, accounting for approximately 10% to 15% of cases [11,12]. Other implicated genes include *BAG3*, *DSP*, and *MYH7*, highlighting PPCM as part of a genetic spectrum of DCM that is unmasked by the hemodynamic and metabolic stresses of pregnancy [11,12].

## Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis
The clinical presentation of PPCM is diverse and often delayed, as early symptoms like dyspnea, fatigue, and peripheral edema overlap with the normal physiological changes of late pregnancy and the early postpartum period [13]. However, rapid progression to orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and cardiogenic shock can occur [13,14].

Echocardiography is the gold standard for diagnosis, demonstrating an LVEF < 45%, often accompanied by left ventricular dilation [15]. Biomarkers play a supportive role; N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) is characteristically elevated and is invaluable for distinguishing PPCM from physiological gestational symptoms, while cardiac troponins can indicate ongoing myocardial injury [16,17]. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging is increasingly utilized to assess myocardial tissue characterization, identify diffuse fibrosis through late gadolinium enhancement, and track long-term ventricular remodeling [18].

## Therapeutic Management
Management requires a multidisciplinary "Heart Team" consisting of obstetricians, cardiologists, neonatologists, and anesthesiologists [19]. Therapeutic strategies differ depending on whether the patient is pregnant or postpartum. During pregnancy, guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) is restricted due to teratogenicity. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs) are strictly contraindicated [20]. Instead, hydralazine and nitrates are used for afterload reduction, alongside beta-blockers (preferably beta-1 selective agents like metoprolol succinate) and loop diuretics for volume management [19,21].

Postpartum, full GDMT should be initiated, including ACE inhibitors/ARBs or sacubitril/valsartan, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs), and beta-blockers [22,23]. Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors are emerging as a key pillar, though data during active breastfeeding remain limited [24]. Anticoagulation is recommended for patients with an LVEF < 35% or those receiving bromocriptine, given the highly prothrombotic state of the peripartum period [25].

Disease-specific therapy targeting the prolactin pathway has transformed PPCM prognosis. Bromocriptine, a dopamine-D2 receptor agonist that blocks prolactin secretion, has shown efficacy in clinical trials [26]. The addition of bromocriptine to standard heart failure therapy (the "BOARD" protocol: Bromocriptine, Oral heart failure therapy, Anticoagulation, vaso-Relaxants, Diuretics) has been shown to enhance LVEF recovery and reduce clinical events [27,28]. For patients presenting with refractory cardiogenic shock, advanced therapies such as mechanical circulatory support (e.g., Impella, venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation) or left ventricular assist devices (LVAD) are critical bridges to recovery or transplantation [29].

## Prognosis and Subsequent Pregnancies
PPCM carries a relatively favorable prognosis compared to other forms of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, with over 50% to 70% of patients experiencing partial or complete recovery of LV function within six months [28,30]. However, patients must be counseled against subsequent pregnancies if their LVEF remains < 50% to 55%, as the risk of relapse, severe heart failure, and mortality is exceedingly high [30]. Even in those with normalized LVEF, subsequent pregnancies carry a 20% risk of recurrence and require close monitoring [30].
